question: What does systolic blood pressure measure in your arteries?

options.A: Total resistance within the peripheral blood vessels
options.C: Average pressure across a full cardiac cycle

explanation: Think of systole as your heart giving a strong squeeze! The systolic pressure is simply the highest point of pressure when the left ventricle contracts and pushes blood out. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why do we measure blood pressure in millimeters of mercury (mmHg)?

options.A: It matches the exact weight of blood inside the left ventricle
options.B: Mercury chemically reacts with blood to show pressure changes
options.C: It reflects the standard height column used in traditional manometers
options.D: The metric system requires all fluid pressures to use liquid units

explanation: Great clinical history here! The 'mmHg' unit comes from old-school mercury blood pressure cuffs where the pressure physically pushed up a column of liquid mercury. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h1)

question: What two main factors determine a patient's overall blood pressure?

options.A: Plasma volume and red blood cell count

explanation: You'll hear this formula a lot in clinicals: Blood Pressure equals Cardiac Output multiplied by Peripheral Resistance. It's the core of how our circulation works! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h2)

question: Where are the quick-acting sensors (baroreceptors) located that help control your blood pressure?

options.D: Right atrium and superior vena cava

explanation: These special stretch receptors sit right in your neck (carotid sinus) and chest (aortic arch) to quickly tell the brain if blood pressure is getting too high or too low. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h2)

question: What range defines a normal, healthy adult blood pressure?
explanation: Keep this rule of thumb close: normal resting blood pressure is generally under 120 for the top number and under 80 for the bottom number. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h3)

question: Why do doctors and nurses usually want multiple high readings before diagnosing hypertension?

options.A: To rule out temporary spikes caused by anxiety or activity
options.B: To ensure the automated blood pressure machine is properly calibrated
options.C: To check if the patient is compliant with daily fluid restrictions
options.D: To calculate the exact lifetime dosage of antihypertensive medication

explanation: Ever noticed your blood pressure goes up when walking into a hospital? That's 'white coat syndrome' or stress! We always double-check before labeling someone hypertensive. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h3)

question: What happens to a blood pressure reading if the cuff you use is too small?

options.B: The systolic and diastolic values disappear

explanation: Always pick the right cuff size! A cuff that's too small squeezes the arm too tightly, making the blood pressure look much higher than it actually is. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h4)

question: What is the correct way to position a patient for an accurate blood pressure check?

options.A: Sitting on the edge of the bed with legs dangling and feet unsupported
options.B: Lying flat on the back with arms resting straight down by the sides
options.C: Standing upright against a wall with arms hanging loosely unsupported
options.D: Sitting with feet flat, back supported, and arm at heart level

explanation: Good posture matters! Letting feet dangle or holding the arm up causes muscle tension, which can throw off your readings. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h4)

question: What is the main feature of essential (primary) hypertension?

options.A: It is always caused by a failing renal artery
options.B: It develops suddenly over a few hours of acute stress
options.C: It responds exclusively to immediate surgical intervention
options.D: It has no single identifiable underlying medical cause

explanation: Most people with high blood pressure have 'primary' hypertension, meaning it builds up slowly over time due to lifestyle and genetics rather than one single disease. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h5)

question: Which of these is a common cause of secondary hypertension?
explanation: When high blood pressure has a clear hidden cause—like kidney or renal artery problems messing with body fluids—we call it secondary hypertension. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h5)

question: How much of a drop in blood pressure defines orthostatic hypotension when someone stands up?

options.A: Drop in systolic of 20 mmHg or more
options.B: Rise in systolic of 30 mmHg or more
options.C: Rise in diastolic of 15 mmHg or more
options.D: Drop in diastolic of 5 mmHg or less

explanation: If a patient stands up and their top number (systolic) drops by 20 mmHg or more, they have orthostatic hypotension. That's why they feel dizzy! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h6)

question: What is the biggest danger of sudden, untreated low blood pressure (hypotension) in the hospital?

options.A: Rapid development of peripheral edema in the lower limbs
options.B: Sudden elevation in intracranial pressure inside the brain
options.C: Inadequate perfusion and oxygenation of vital organs
options.D: Severe permanent thickening of the left ventricular wall

explanation: When pressure drops too low, blood stops flowing well to vital organs like the brain and kidneys. Without enough oxygen, the body can slip into shock. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h6)

question: Which of these is a key lifestyle change for managing high blood pressure without drugs?
explanation: Cutting down on salt (sodium) helps the body hold onto less water, lowering the pressure inside blood vessels naturally. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h7)

question: What common side effect should you watch out for in patients taking ACE inhibitors?
explanation: ACE inhibitors (like lisinopril) are fantastic for blood pressure, but they often trigger a harmless, nagging dry cough in many patients. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h7)

question: What happens to the heart muscle over time when high blood pressure goes untreated?
explanation: Just like lifting weights makes your biceps bigger, the left ventricle gets thick and overworked because it has to constantly push against high resistance in the arteries. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h8)

question: Why does long-term, uncontrolled high blood pressure often lead to kidney disease?

options.A: High pressure prevents the bladder from emptying its contents fully
options.B: High pressure damages and scars the delicate glomerular blood vessels
options.C: The ureters become permanently constricted by high fluid pressure
options.D: Excess blood volume dissolves the nephrons inside the renal medulla

explanation: The tiny filtering blood vessels in the kidneys take a serious beating from high pressure, which scars them over time and leads to kidney failure. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h8)

question: Why do nurses always remind patients that high blood pressure is often a 'silent killer' (asymptomatic)?

options.A: Patients can safely ignore occasional high clinic readings
options.B: Patients only need treatment when they experience severe headaches
options.C: Patients might stop taking medications if they feel fine
options.D: Patients will not need any more blood pressure checks

explanation: Because high blood pressure doesn't always cause pain or headaches, patients often feel great and mistakenly stop taking their life-saving medications. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h9)

question: What is the best home-care advice a nurse can give a patient who is monitoring their blood pressure?

options.A: Keep a written log of daily readings to share at clinic visits
options.B: Calibrate the digital home machine using household kitchen scales
options.C: Measure the blood pressure immediately after strenuous exercise
options.D: Adjust medication dosages independently based on daily numbers

explanation: A written diary is a nurse's best friend! It gives the doctor a clear picture of how the patient is doing during normal everyday life. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h9)
